topics.title: One Phone Call Doubled the Load on This Walkway

demand.family: Bridge, dam or building: every corner cut

topics.hook: Hundreds were dancing in the hotel atrium. Above them hung two walkways on thin steel rods.
cause_chain: The original design hangs the 4th- and 2nd-floor walkways from one continuous rod per hanger
Even that connection reaches only about 60% of what the building code expected
During construction the fabricator asks, by phone, to switch to two offset rods; the change goes through without full checks
The 4th-floor box beams now carry both walkways, roughly double the load; during a tea dance the connections pull through
topics.rule_after: NBS BSS 143 (1982); the engineers lost their licences, and the profession made the structural engineer of record responsible for connection design and shop-drawing review.
topics.human_moment: Rescuers worked through the night to free people trapped under the fallen walkways.

outline: Hook (0-45 s): the atrium full on 17 Jul 1981, two stacked walkways on roof rods; 7:05 the upper one gives way onto the lower and both fall; steel and workmanship were not the cause (NBS conclusion 9); promise: a weak detail, a rod change, a review that missed it
1 The hotel: opened 1980; glass atrium; three walkways (2nd/4th stacked, 3rd offset), no columns, hung on rods; dance event, crowd 1,500-2,000 at 7:00 PM

2 The design: box beam = two 8-inch channels welded toe to toe; rod through the beam, washer and nut under it; one continuous rod roof-4th-2nd; even this would reach ~60% of the code's expected capacity

3 The change: fabricator's shop drawings use two rods, the lower set offset 4 in; request by phone, approved verbally (as reported; the firm disputed it); stamped as reviewed; the 4th-floor connection's load essentially doubled

4 The last minutes (MissionClock): 7:00 crowd; 63 people on the 2nd/4th walkways (news videotape); 7:04 band back for the dance contest; max load only 31% of the code-expected capacity; from day one barely able to carry their own weight

5 The failure (3D hero cutaway): connection 9UE, east end of the 4th-floor middle box beam; flanges rotate, lower weld splits, rod pulls through; neighbours fail; 4th drops onto 2nd, both fall; 7:08 first call; 113 dead, 186 injured (one beat)

6 The findings: NBS arrives 21 Jul; weighed spans (dead load ~8% over nominal), lab mock-ups; 302 kN expected vs 83 kN average; two factors; with the original rods the 3rd-floor walkway (53%) would have been weakest

7 What changed: Missouri board revoked two engineers' licences (gross negligence, misconduct); ASCE Oct 1985 policy: the engineer of record is responsible for all steel design including connections; payoff: they fell at 31% of what the code expected; ask: which link should have been caught first?

topics.title: The Gauge Said Normal. The Tower Was Nearly Full.
topics.hook: The gauge said the tower's level was fine. It was filling to the top.
cause_chain: During start-up, operators fill the raffinate splitter tower far above its normal level; the level reading is wrong
The tower overfills and over-pressurises; relief valves send liquid to an old blowdown drum
The drum vents straight to the air through a stack; a 1992 OSHA citation about a similar drum was dropped and it was never tied to a flare
Flammable liquid erupts from the stack, forms a vapour cloud and ignites among contractors' trailers parked nearby
topics.rule_after: CSB urgent recommendations (25 Oct 2005): API to write new guidelines so occupied trailers sit safely away from hazardous process areas (API agreed), and an industry safety alert; final report Mar 2007 on blowdown stacks, alarms and fatigue.
topics.human_moment: The 15 who died were contract workers in or near trailers placed close to the unit for convenience.

topics.title: One Unit Mistake Lost a $125M Spacecraft
topics.hook: One file used pounds where it should have used newtons, and a $125 million spacecraft flew into Mars's air at 57 kilometres.
cause_chain: The interface spec says newton-seconds
The ground 'Small Forces' file writes pound-seconds
Thruster pushes are 10-14x more frequent than planned, so the 4.45x underestimate builds up
Navigation discrepancies are reported only informally and TCM-5 is not executed
topics.rule_after: NASA Mishap Investigation Board (Phase I, 10 Nov 1999): end-to-end verification of software interfaces and units, and a formal path for engineers to escalate concerns.
topics.human_moment: Navigators had noticed the trajectory didn't fit, and said so, but the worry never stopped the mission.

verify: All board figures from the MIB Phase I report pp. 6 and 13-14 (read 2026-11-23): launch 11 Dec 1998; MOI 23 Sep 1999 09:00:46 UTC; LOS 09:04:52, 49 s early; 226 km planned, 150-170 km in the week before, as low as 110 km one hour before, 80 km survivable, 57 km afterwards (p. 14)

Root cause in the board's words (p. 6, 16): failure to use metric units in the ground software file 'Small Forces'; the AMD file was delivered in lbf-s instead of the SIS's N-s, underestimating the effect by 4.45 (code computes 4.448 from physics)
Contributing: working-level navigation discrepancies 'only informally reported', Doppler-only solutions consistently closer, TCM-5 discussed verbally but not executed (pp. 13, 18-19)
$125M cost is from Physics Today, not the board report: label it 'Data: Physics Today'
Name no individual engineers; the board names the units, the file and the process, and both teams (spacecraft team, Colorado; navigation team, JPL)
topics.search: mars climate orbiter metric error explained
outline: Hook (0-15 s, owner 2026-11-22: small cause + scale first): 23 Sep 1999, 09:04:52 UTC, the orbiter slips behind Mars 49 s early and never comes back; one file in pounds instead of newtons, a $125M spacecraft, 57 km instead of 226 km; promise: four chances to catch it, and all four missed

1 The mission (0:15-1:30): launched 11 Dec 1998, a weather satellite for Mars and relay for the Polar Lander; picture the whole video hangs on: a thread of trajectory from Earth to Mars that drifts a hair every few days
2 How it was meant to work (flat diagram): reaction wheels spin up, small thrusters dump the momentum (AMD events), each push is reported to the navigators in newton-seconds per the interface spec

3 The leak: the 'Small Forces' file reports pound-seconds; every push looks 4.45x smaller than it was (code: 1 lbf = 4.448 N); the asymmetric solar array means AMD events 10-14 times more often than planned, so the error piles up; cliffhanger: the navigators noticed
4 The warnings (recap-and-tease at ~4:00): Doppler-only fixes kept saying 'closer'; concerns only informally reported; 226 km becomes 150-170 km in the final week

5 The last hour (MissionClock + altitude gauge): tracking says as low as 110 km, survival line 80 km; TCM-5 discussed verbally, not executed; 09:00:46 engine start, 09:04:52 loss of signal, 21 min of silence that never ends
6 The finding: 29 Sep, the factor of 4.45 is found; corrected estimate 57 km, inside the air; the report page with 'failure to use metric units' highlighted
7 What changed: the board's recommendations for the Polar Lander (verify small-forces models, a TCM-5 plan and readiness); ending ask: which of the four checks should have caught it first?

topics.title: Why Airline Pilots Now Need 1,500 Hours

demand.family: Air crash, minute by minute, ending on the rule

topics.hook: A stall warning on a calm night approach to Buffalo, one pull back on the controls, and 27 seconds later 50 people were dead. It changed how every US airline pilot is trained.
cause_chain: A regional Q400 approaches Buffalo at night in icing; the crew chats through the approach
Airspeed decays unnoticed; the stick shaker warns of a stall
The captain pulls back instead of pushing forward; the aircraft stalls and rolls
Training, fatigue and the airline's procedures had left the crew unprepared for that moment
topics.rule_after: Airline Safety and FAA Extension Act of 2010 (signed 1 Aug 2010): airline first officers need an ATP certificate with 1,500 hours (in force 1 Aug 2013), plus new fatigue rules and stall-recovery training.
topics.human_moment: The victims' families lobbied Congress for more than a year until the law passed.

Probable cause in the NTSB's words: 'the captain's inappropriate response to the activation of the stick shaker'; four contributing factors incl. airspeed monitoring, sterile cockpit, and Colgan's icing airspeed procedures. outline: Hook (0-15 s): the stall warning, one pull back, 27 s, 50 dead; the twist: the plane was flying fine; promise: why one reflex rewrote US pilot rules
1 The flight (0:15-1:30): Continental Connection 3407, a Q400 turboprop, Newark to Buffalo on a winter night, clear enough to see the lights; ice detected, the de-icing on
2 How it should work (flat diagram): the low-speed cue rises in icing; the stick shaker warns before a stall; the trained response is nose down, power up
3 The chain, one link per beat: airspeed briefed 118 kt; casual talk below 10,000 ft (sterile cockpit); gear down, flaps called, speed bleeds to 131 kt while the cue climbs, nobody calls it
4 Recap-and-tease (~4:00): three small lapses so far, the fourth takes under a second

5 The last 27 seconds (MissionClock + airspeed tape): 2216:27.4 shaker; 2216:27.8 the column comes back; 45° roll; pusher pushes, is overpowered; flaps up; 2216:54 the recording ends; the house in Clarence Center, 5 nm out; 49 aboard and 1 on the ground (one beat)
6 The findings: the report page, probable cause highlighted; fatigue and commuting discussed but not proven; 25 recommendations

7 What changed (the families' campaign as fact, not drama): 2010 Act, 1,500 hours for airline first officers, new rest rules and stall training; ending ask: rule, reflex or rest, which one would you have fixed first?

topics.title: The Ferry That Sailed With Its Doors Open
topics.hook: One man asleep in his cabin, one bow door left open, and four minutes after a ferry passed the harbour wall at Zeebrugge, 193 people were dead.
cause_chain: The assistant bosun, whose job is to close the bow doors, is asleep when the ferry leaves Zeebrugge
The officer meant to check assumes it's done; the master has no indicator and no report
Company standing orders say nothing about the doors; bow-down and speeding up, the ship takes the sea onto the open car deck
Water on the undivided vehicle deck destroys her stability and she capsizes
topics.rule_after: Sheen formal investigation (1987): bow-door indicator lights and monitoring on ro-ro ferries and stronger stability rules; the company-wide failings it found were a major reason for the IMO's ISM Code, the safety-management system every ship operator must run.
topics.human_moment: Passengers and crew formed human chains and ladders to pull people up out of the flooded ship.

2 How it was meant to work (flat diagram): the bow doors close at harbour stations; the bridge has no way to see them; the system is 'someone would have said'
3 The chain: the Zeebrugge berth needs the ship trimmed by the head; the man whose job it is falls asleep; the officer who should check leaves for the bridge; nobody reports, because nobody has to
4 Recap-and-tease (~3:30): it had happened before, on a sister ship in 1983

5 The four minutes (MissionClock + speed gauge + bow-height cutaway in 3D): past the mole, 14 kt to 18 kt, squat and bow wave, water over the spade onto the car deck; free surface rolls her; she lands on a sandbank on her side
6 The findings: the 1985 memo asking for a light on the bridge, and the replies (on-screen transcript); 'the disease of sloppiness' highlighted on the report page
7 What changed: indicator lights fitted after the disaster; the MAIB formed in 1989; ending ask: one light, one alarm, one checklist: which should have come first?

topics.title: The Parked Train That Rolled Into Town
topics.hook: Seven hand brakes on a train that needed at least seventeen: shortly before 1 a.m. it rolled 7.2 miles downhill into Lac-Mégantic at 65 miles an hour, and 47 people died.
cause_chain: A one-person crew parks a crude-oil train on a downhill main line and sets too few hand brakes
The test meant to prove the hand brakes hold is done with the air brakes still applied
A locomotive fire is put out by shutting the engine down, so the air brakes slowly bleed off
The train rolls downhill into town and 63 tank cars derail in the centre
topics.rule_after: TSB R13D0054 (Aug 2014): Canada required physical defences against runaways, stricter hand-brake rules, two-person crews for dangerous goods, tougher tank-car standards and audited safety management.
topics.human_moment: It was a summer Friday night; the Musi-Café bar in the town centre was full.
topics.angle: Open at the moment of failure with a date/place/speed caption, cut back, walk the cause chain step by step with the physics, hold the toll for a turn, end on the rule that changed (named and dated).

1 The train (0:15-1:30): 72 tank cars of crude, 5 locomotives, one person crew, parked for the night at Nantes on the main line above the town; the picture the video hangs on: a slope with a train held by a handful of wheels
2 How it was meant to work (flat diagram): air brakes leak off over hours; hand brakes are mechanical and permanent; the rule: enough hand brakes to hold the train with no air at all
3 The chain: 7 hand brakes set; the test is run with the locomotive air brakes still on, so it passes; the lead locomotive, poorly repaired, is left running to keep air
4 Recap-and-tease (~3:30): the train is safe only while one engine keeps running

5 The night (MissionClock + air-pressure gauge + speed gauge): the engine catches fire; it is shut down; air pressure bleeds away; ~01:00 the train moves; 7.2 miles; 65 mph at the curve in town; 63 tank cars derail, fire (3D, the derailing bogie, no victims)
6 The findings: 18 cause factors; the report page with the hand-brake test finding highlighted; 17 vs 7 as a gauge

7 What changed: Canada's rules on securing unattended trains, crew size and tank-car standards (name and date each from the TSB/Transport Canada pages); ending ask: which of the 18 should have been the first to stop it?

topics.title: How a Badly Built Drain Derailed a Train at 73 mph
topics.hook: Nine people on a train told the line was fine. At 73 miles an hour it hit gravel washed out of a drain that was never built to its drawing, and three of them died.
cause_chain: 2011-12: the drain above the line is built, but not to the design: a low bund nobody designed sends the slope's water into one spot
Nobody refers the changes to the designer, no as-built drawings exist, and the upper drain never enters the maintenance database, so it is never inspected
12 Aug 2020: 51.5 mm of rain between 05:50 and 09:00; the train, stopped by a landslip ahead, waits over two hours to turn back
Between about 08:15 and 09:00 gravel washes out of a 15 m length of the steep drain onto the rails; nobody knows
No process tells the train to run slowly after the storm; the signaller says the line is fine; at 73 mph it hits the debris, derails and strikes a bridge parapet
topics.rule_after: RAIB report 02/2022 (10 March 2022), 20 recommendations: Network Rail's extreme-weather operations, drainage asset records and control of construction changes.
topics.human_moment: The train had already been turned back once that morning; it was on its way back to the safety of Stonehaven station.

topics.title: Why a Train Ran a Red Signal While Its Driver Texted
topics.hook: Twenty-two seconds after the engineer's last text message, his commuter train met a freight train head-on. Twenty-five people died, and a system that could have stopped it already existed.
cause_chain: A Metrolink commuter train and a Union Pacific freight share a single track; the freight is to wait in a siding at Control Point Topanga
The Metrolink engineer, on duty, is sending and receiving text messages, which the rules forbid
Leaving Chatsworth, the train should keep under 40 mph and be ready to stop; it passes the red signal at Topanga at 44 mph
It runs through the switch; 21 seconds with no brake or throttle change; no positive train control exists to stop it
The two trains meet head-on at about 43 and 41 mph; the locomotive is driven 52 feet into the first coach
topics.rule_after: The Rail Safety Improvement Act of 2008, passed weeks later, required positive train control by 31 Dec 2015; the FRA's Emergency Order 26 made crew use of wireless devices a federal violation (NTSB RAR-10/01, adopted 21 Jan 2010).
topics.human_moment: It was a Friday afternoon commute home; people on the Chatsworth platform saw the signal ahead showing green as the train left, because it was still set for the freight's siding.

topics.title: Why Every Airliner Toilet Now Has a Smoke Detector

demand.family: Air crash, minute by minute, ending on the rule

topics.hook: A fire behind the back toilet of a jet at 33,000 feet, in a room with no smoke detector. The plane landed. About a minute after the doors opened, the cabin flashed over, and 23 people never got out.
cause_chain: 18:51: three circuit breakers for the aft lavatory trip at cruise; crews think a popped lavatory breaker is routine
There is no smoke detector in the lavatory; smoke is found only around 19:00, by a passenger in the last row
The crew is told the smoke is clearing; minutes pass before the emergency descent begins
Electrical systems fail; the DC-9 lands at Cincinnati at 19:20:09
60 to 90 seconds after the exits open, a flash fire fills the cabin
topics.rule_after: NTSB AAR-86/02 (adopted 31 Jan 1986; first adopted 8 Aug 1984). FAA proposals that followed: NPRM 83-15 floor-path lighting visible under smoke; NPRM 84-5 lavatory smoke detectors and automatic waste-bin extinguishers; NPRM 83-14 tougher cabin flammability.
topics.human_moment: A passenger in the last row noticed the smell first and asked a flight attendant; Canadian folk singer Stan Rogers was among those lost (verify).
